ranking.rationale: Age is one of the most robust and semantically stable predictors of cholesterol risk across NHANES domains, reflecting underlying biology rather than survey wave or access-to-care artifacts. It offers strong marginal signal without directly encoding domain identifiers or brittle shortcuts.

Sex is a strong, biologically stable determinant of cholesterol patterns and cardiovascular risk, adding broad predictive signal complementary to age while being less likely than survey year, birthplace, education, or diagnosis-history variables to encode domain shift, healthcare access, or leakage.

Hypertension is a strong, biologically linked correlate of high cholesterol and cardiovascular risk that should remain predictive across NHANES domain shifts. It adds substantial signal beyond age and sex while being less likely than year, birthplace, education, or marital status to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

Self-reported diabetes status is a strong, biologically stable correlate of cholesterol risk beyond age, sex, and high blood pressure, reflecting metabolic dysfunction rather than domain-specific artifacts. It should generalize better across NHANES shifts than year, birthplace, education, or marital-status variables, while adding more direct cardiovascular risk information than the other comorbidity candidates.

Education adds stable socioeconomic signal for cholesterol risk beyond age, sex, hypertension, and diabetes. It is broadly causal via diet, healthcare access, and health behaviors, and is less likely than survey year or birthplace to act mainly as a domain identifier or brittle shortcut.

Arthritis adds stable health-status information linked to systemic inflammation, reduced activity, obesity, and cardiometabolic risk, so it should remain semantically predictive of cholesterol across NHANES domains. It is less likely than survey year or birthplace to encode domain shifts, and likely offers broader, less sparse signal than kidney failure, dialysis, psoriasis, prediabetes, or marital status given age, sex, diabetes, blood-pressure history, and education are already selected.

Kidney disease is a clinically meaningful comorbidity that remains stably associated with abnormal cholesterol through shared cardiometabolic risk and treatment pathways, adding signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, education, and heart-condition history. It is less likely than survey year or birthplace to encode domain shifts, and less redundant or access-to-care dependent than prediabetes.

Prediabetes history adds stable metabolic-risk information closely tied to cholesterol beyond age, sex, diagnosed diabetes, education, hypertension, heart disease, and kidney weakness. It is more semantically relevant and likely to generalize across NHANES domains than year, birthplace, or marital status, and less sparse/extreme than dialysis or psoriasis.

Marital status adds plausible, relatively stable signal for cholesterol risk through household structure, stress, and health behaviors beyond age, sex, education, diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease. It is less likely than survey year or country of birth to act as a domain identifier, and likely offers broader marginal utility than rare-condition indicators like dialysis or psoriasis.

Psoriasis adds plausible stable clinical signal through chronic systemic inflammation and cardiometabolic risk, with less direct domain-shift or demographic-shortcut risk than year or country-of-birth. Dialysis is highly predictive but likely too rare and brittle for broad marginal gain after existing comorbidity features.

Dialysis is a strong clinical indicator of severe kidney disease, which has a biologically plausible and generally stable association with abnormal cholesterol risk beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, education, and cardiovascular history. It is more semantically tied to health status than country of birth, and far less likely than survey year to encode domain shift or spurious benchmark-specific differences.

Country of birth may add modest, semantically relevant signal through stable differences in lifetime diet, healthcare access, and cardiometabolic risk beyond age, sex, education, and comorbidities. In contrast, survey year is primarily a domain indicator in TableShift and is likely to encode spurious train/test differences rather than stable biology, so it should be strongly penalized.

Only remaining candidate. It likely acts primarily as a survey-wave/domain identifier rather than a stable causal predictor of cholesterol, so its marginal value for robust OOD generalization is low or potentially harmful, but it must be selected from the available set.
